• Based on the effect of mutations on protein synthesis mutations can be
  • A. Silent mutation
  • A silent mutation changes a codon without changing the amino acid it encodes. Silent mutations
  • often have little effect on protein sequence, although some can influence splicing, mRNA
  • stability or translation efficiency.
  • Example: In the coding DNA strand, a change from GAA to GAG changes the codon but both
  • specify glutamic acid in the standard genetic code.
  • B. Missense mutation
  • A missense mutation changes a codon so that a different amino acid is incorporated into the
  • protein. Significance: Missense mutations may alter protein folding, stability or function. Their
  • effects range from negligible to severe.
  • Example: In sickle-cell disease, a mutation in the β-globin gene changes the glutamic acid
  • codon to a valine codon in the β-globin protein.
  • C. Nonsense mutation
  • A nonsense mutation converts an amino acid codon into a stop codon (UAA, UAG and UGA).
  • Translation may terminate prematurely, producing a shortened protein that is often non -
  • functional. Some affected mRNAs are also degraded by cellular quality-control mechanisms.
  • D. Frameshift mutations
  • A frameshift mutation occurs when a nucleotide insertion or deletion changes the reading frame
  • of a coding sequence. Such a mutation generally causes a frameshift when the number of
  • inserted or deleted nucleotides is not a multiple of three.
  • Example:
  • In an mRNA with o riginal coding sequence: AUG-AAA-GGC-UUU if deletion of one
  • nucleotide occurs at the 5’ end the coding sequence will be UGA- AAG-GCU- UU
  • After a one-nucleotide insertion or deletion, the grouping of downstream codons changes.
  • Frame shift mutation can
  • ➢ Can alter the downstream amino acid sequence.

questions.solution_html:
• Based on origin mutations can be
  • Spontaneous and induced point mutations
  • Spontaneous mutations: Arise naturally due to replication errors, spontaneous chemical
  • changes in bases or errors in DNA repair.
  • Induced mutations: Result from exposure to mutagens, including certain chemicals and
  • ultraviolet or ionizing radiation.
  • Biological significance of point mutations
  • Point mutations have several important biological consequences.
  • ➢ Genetic variation: They introduce new alleles into populations.
  • ➢ Evolution: Beneficial mutations can contribute to adaptation and natural selection.
  • ➢ Genetic disorders: Mutations in essential genes may cause inherited diseases.
  • ➢ Cancer: Mutations in genes regulating cell division, DNA repair and cell survival can
  • contribute to tumour formation.
  • ➢ Protein function: Mutations may alter protein structure, activity or stability.
  • ➢ Molecular research: Experimentally induced point mutations help researchers identify
  • the functions of genes and specific amino acids in proteins.
  • Point mutations are small-scale changes in DNA that may have neutral, harmful or beneficial
  • effects. Transitions and transversions describe the types of base substitutions, while silent,
  • missense and nonsense mutations describe their effects on protein cod ing. Frameshift
  • mutations caused by single-nucleotide insertions or deletions can also profoundly affect protein
  • synthesis. Point mutations are important in genetic variation, evolution, disease and molecular
  • biology research.

questions.question: Explain the significance of conserved genes and proteins citing suitable examples. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the significance of conserved genes and proteins, citing suitable examples.
  • Ans: Conserved genes and proteins are genes and proteins that have remained relatively
  • unchanged during evolution because they perform essential biological functions. They are
  • important tools for understanding cellular functions and evolutionary relationships.
  • Significance:
  • ➢ Essential cellular functions: Conserved genes encode proteins necessary for basic
  • cellular processes.
  • ➢ Evidence of evolution: Similar genes and proteins in different organisms indicate
  • common ancestry.
  • ➢ Phylogenetic studies: Conserved sequences help establish evolutionary relationships.
  • ➢ Identification of organisms: DNA sequence comparisons can help identify species.
  • ➢ Research applications: Conserved genes provide useful models for studying gene
  • function and disease mechanisms.
  • Examples:
  • ➢ Ribosomal RNA genes are conserved because they are essential for protein synthesis.
  • ➢ Histone proteins are conserved because they package and organize DNA.
  • ➢ Cytochrome c is involved in cellular respiration and has been used in evolutionary
  • comparisons.
  • ➢ ATP synthase proteins are conserved because they participate in ATP production.

questions.question: Illustrate and explain the salivary gland chromosome. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate and explain the salivary gland chromosome.
  • Ans: Salivary gland chromosomes, also called polytene chromosomes, are giant chromosomes
  • found in the salivary gland cells of certain dipteran insect larvae, such as Drosophila. They are
  • formed due to the repeated rounds of DNA replication occur in the salivary gland cells without
  • cell division. The replicated chromatids remain aligned, forming giant chromosomes. They
  • show bands and interbands. Dark bands contain densely packed ch romatin, while lighter
  • interbands contain less densely packed chromatin. The regions which are at active gene
  • transcription become enlarged due to local chromatin decondensation and are known as
  • chromosomal puffs. These prominent puffs with intense RNA synthesis are known as Balbiani
  • rings. Salivary gland chromosomes were used in studying chromosome organization, gene
  • activity.

questions.question: Describe the wobble hypothesis proposed by Crick. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the wobble hypothesis proposed by Crick.
  • Ans: The wobble hypothesis, proposed by Francis Crick in 1966, explains how a single tRNA
  • molecule can recognize more than one codon during protein synthesis/ more than one code for
  • the same amino acid. This is known as the degeneracy of the codon.
  • According to woble hypothesis, the first two bases of the codon generally form specific base
  • pairs with the corresponding bases of the tRNA anticodon but the third base at the codon's 3′
  • end can show flexibility in pairing with the first base at the anticodon's 5′ end. This is called
  • wobble pairing. Thus explains the degeneracy of the genetic code. Due to Wobble pairing single
  • tRNA can recognize multiple synonymous codons that specify the same amino acid. This
  • reduces the number of different tRNA molecules required for translation.

questions.question: Discuss how the cytoskeleton helps in cell structure and function. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss how the cytoskeleton helps in cell structure and function.
  • Ans: The cytoskeleton is a dynamic network of protein filaments that provides structural
  • support and essential for intracellular movement, transport and accurate cell division. The
  • major components and functions of cytoskeleton are given below.
  • ➢ Microtubules: Made of tubulin. They maintain cell organization, form the mitotic
  • spindle, and participate in intracellular transport and the structure of cilia and flagella.
  • ➢ Microfilaments: Made mainly of actin. They help maintain cell shape, support
  • cytoplasmic streaming and contribute to cell movement and cytokinesis.
  • ➢ Intermediate filaments: Provide mechanical strength and help resist cellular stress in
  • organisms that possess them. Plant cells do not have the typical cytoplasmic
  • intermediate-filament system characteristic of animal cells.
  • ➢ Cell division: Microtubules organize the spindle that separates chromosomes during
  • mitosis.
  • ➢ Intracellular transport: Cytoskeletal tracks enable motor proteins to transport vesicles
  • and organelles.
  • ➢ Plant cell organization : The cortical cytoskeleton helps guide cellulose synthase
  • complexes and thereby influences the orientation of cellulose microfibrils in the cell
  • wall.

questions.question: DNA repair mechanisms in cells are essential for the normal well-being of an organism. Why? / [CO6]
questions.solution_html:
• DNA repair mechanisms in cells are essential for the normal well-being of an organism.
  • Why?
  • Ans: In every organism DNA is continuously exposed to damage from ultraviolet radiation,
  • chemicals, reactive oxygen species and errors during DNA replication. DNA repair
  • mechanisms correct this damage and preserve genetic stability.
  • The significance of DNA repair mechanisms include
  • ➢ Maintenance of genetic information: Repair mechanisms restore damaged DNA and
  • preserve the integrity of the genome.
  • ➢ Prevention of mutations: They reduce the accumulation of permanent changes in DNA
  • sequences.
  • ➢ Prevention of cancer: Repair of DNA damage in genes controlling cell growth helps
  • reduce the risk of cancer.
  • ➢ Normal cell functioning: DNA repair enables accurate replication and expression of
  • genetic information.
  • ➢ Cell survival: Repair of potentially lethal DNA damage supports cell viability.
  • ➢ Reproductive and developmental health: DNA repair helps maintain genome integrity
  • in germ cells and developing tissues.
  • ➢ Ageing and disease prevention: Defects in repair systems can contribute to premature
  • ageing, developmental abnormalities and genetic disorders.
